messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi is a 45-year-old man of African descent who works as an agricultural laborer on a mid-sized farm in the rural South. He came to the clinic at the insistence of his partner, who had watched him grow increasingly withdrawn and unreachable over the past two years. His PCL-5 score of 48 places him firmly in the clinical range for PTSD, though the roots of his distress reach back more than three decades, to a childhood spent in a household where violence was a recurring presence.

Kofi was nine years old the first time he crouched behind the thin plywood door of his bedroom and listened to his father beat his mother. He remembers the specific sounds — the crack of an open palm, his mother's muffled pleading, the way the silence afterward felt heavier than the noise. He did not go out. He stayed behind that door, small and motionless, and that stillness has never entirely left him. Over the years the violence continued, and so did his inaction, and he had come to believe that his failure to intervene — even as a child, even when he had no power — was a moral failure he could never undo. He will never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. That conviction is not abstract; it surfaces in the middle of the workday, while he is moving irrigation lines alone between rows of cotton, replaying scenarios in which he imagines confronting his father, or worse, imagines what he might do to him now. He ruminates obsessively about getting even, constructing and reconstructing acts of retribution that never arrive at resolution and leave him more agitated than before.

These appraisals — that he is fundamentally guilty, that people cannot be trusted, that whatever happiness he once had is permanently behind him — have quietly organized his experience of threat. Because he has come to see himself as someone who failed to protect, and the world as a place where harm is always imminent and people are never reliably safe, he moves through his days in a state of sustained alertness. On the farm, where he works alongside a small rotating crew, he is superalert in a way that exhausts him: tracking where each coworker is positioned, reading tone of voice, watching hands. At night the vigilance intensifies. His partner has described lying beside a man who does not sleep so much as patrol the dark, and Kofi himself acknowledges that the hours between midnight and dawn feel genuinely dangerous in a way he cannot rationalize away. Even when she tells him he is safe, he finds it impossible to believe her.

In response to this unrelenting sense of danger, Kofi has built a set of behavioral rules that feel to him like reasonable precautions. The most rigid is that he will not allow himself to be alone with another person — not a coworker in a storage shed, not a neighbor who stops by, not even a family member in a closed room. On the farm this has created real friction; his supervisor has twice commented on his refusal to ride in the cab of a truck with a single colleague, and Kofi has deflected with excuses that are wearing thin. He also works hard to suppress any thought of the trauma itself, pushing images away the moment they surface. But these strategies, rather than quieting the alarm, have tightened it. The effort of constant suppression keeps the material close and primed, and the hypervigilance that the avoidance was meant to manage has only deepened — each precaution confirming to him that the threat is real enough to require such extraordinary measures. And over time, the isolation these behaviors have produced has fed back into his darkest beliefs about himself: that he is broken, that he has lost his faith in people and in any ordering principle in life, that the misery he now carries is simply who he is.

What finally brought Kofi in was a moment last spring when, after refusing to enter the equipment barn with a coworker, he sat alone in a field and could not stop crying and did not know why. He is not sure what he hopes for. He is most afraid, he said quietly, that there is no version of himself that is not this.
